question: Under Missouri law (RSMo 306.220), what is required of any child under age 7 aboard a watercraft on Missouri waters?
choice_a: The child must wear a U.S. Coast Guard-approved personal flotation device unless in a fully enclosed area designed to prevent falling overboard
choice_b: The child must sit in the center of the boat at all times, with no PFD required
choice_c: The child must be belowdecks whenever the boat is underway
choice_d: There is no PFD requirement for any child under Missouri law
explanation: Missouri law requires every child under age 7 aboard a watercraft on state waters to wear a USCG-approved personal flotation device, unless the child is inside a fully enclosed area of the vessel designed to prevent them from falling overboard or being ejected; violating this is a class C misdemeanor.
source_note: RSMo 306.220 (personal flotation device requirement, children under seven)

question: What class of offense is it in Missouri to allow a child under 7 aboard a watercraft without a required, properly worn PFD?
choice_c: No offense at all -- it is only a recommendation
choice_d: A civil infraction with no criminal penalty
explanation: RSMo 306.220 makes it a class C misdemeanor to permit a child under age 7 to be aboard a watercraft on Missouri waters without wearing an approved PFD, absent the fully enclosed area exception.
source_note: RSMo 306.220 (penalty for children under seven without a PFD)

question: Which PFD types are approved for all persons aboard a personal watercraft (PWC) under Missouri law (RSMo 306.142)?
choice_a: Only inflatable Type III belt packs
choice_b: Any flotation cushion, whether or not it is Coast Guard-approved
choice_c: Type I, Type II, Type III, or Type V U.S. Coast Guard-approved personal flotation devices
choice_d: PFDs are not required on a PWC in Missouri
explanation: Missouri's PWC statute requires every person aboard a personal watercraft to wear a Coast Guard-approved Type I, II, III, or V personal flotation device -- inflatable belt-pack PFDs generally do not qualify unless specifically approved for PWC use while worn as designed.

question: How many wearable PFDs must a Missouri Class 1 vessel (16 to less than 26 feet) carry under RSMo 306.100?
choice_a: Exactly two PFDs regardless of the number of people aboard
choice_b: None -- PFDs are optional on any vessel over 16 feet
choice_c: Only a throwable cushion, with no wearable PFDs required
choice_d: At least one wearable Type I, II, or III PFD for each person on board, plus one throwable Type IV device
explanation: Missouri's equipment statute requires vessels other than Class A to carry one wearable Type I, II, or III PFD per person aboard, plus at least one throwable Type IV device; the wearable devices must be Coast Guard-approved, in serviceable condition, and readily accessible.
source_note: RSMo 306.100 (PFD carriage requirements by vessel class)

question: What is the main functional difference between a Type I and a Type III PFD?
choice_a: A Type I offshore life jacket is designed to turn most unconscious wearers face-up in the water and provides the most buoyancy, while a Type III flotation aid is more comfortable for continuous wear but will not reliably turn an unconscious person face-up
choice_b: A Type I is only for children, while a Type III is only for adults
choice_c: There is no functional difference; the numbers only indicate color
choice_d: A Type III provides more buoyancy than a Type I
explanation: Type I offshore life jackets offer the most buoyancy and are designed to turn most unconscious wearers face-up, making them suited to remote or rough water where rescue may be delayed; Type III flotation aids are more comfortable for activities like fishing or water sports but offer less turning ability.
source_note: Universal boating safety fundamentals (USCG PFD type classifications)

question: What is a Type IV PFD, and how must it be used?
choice_a: A wearable jacket meant only for children under 30 pounds
choice_b: A throwable device, such as a ring buoy or buoyant cushion, intended to be thrown to a person in the water rather than worn
choice_c: A device that never needs to be Coast Guard-approved
explanation: A Type IV PFD is a throwable device, such as a ring buoy or buoyant cushion, designed to be thrown to a conscious person in the water and grasped until rescued; it is a supplement to, not a substitute for, wearable PFDs.
source_note: Universal boating safety fundamentals (USCG PFD type classifications)

question: What is a Type V PFD?
choice_a: A device with unlimited approved uses regardless of the label
choice_b: A device intended exclusively for use by pets
choice_c: A special-use device (such as an inflatable belt pack, deck suit, or work vest) that is only Coast Guard-approved for the specific activity listed on its label, and often only counts as a substitute for a Type I, II, or III PFD if worn as required by its label
explanation: Type V PFDs are special-use devices, such as inflatable belt packs or deck suits, approved only for the conditions specified on their label; many must be worn (not just carried) to count toward a vessel's PFD requirement.
source_note: Universal boating safety fundamentals (USCG PFD type classifications)

question: According to boating safety course guidance, what condition must a PFD be in to satisfy carriage requirements?
choice_a: Any personal flotation device regardless of condition, as long as it is on board somewhere
choice_b: Locked in a cabin compartment that cannot be reached while underway
choice_c: Only required to be Coast Guard-approved; fit and condition do not matter
choice_d: U.S. Coast Guard-approved, in serviceable condition (no rips, waterlogging, or broken straps), the correct size for the wearer, and readily accessible
explanation: A PFD only satisfies legal and practical safety requirements if it is Coast Guard-approved, properly sized for the intended wearer, in good serviceable condition, and stored so it can be reached quickly in an emergency -- a PFD buried under gear does no good in a capsizing.
source_note: Universal boating safety fundamentals (PFD condition and accessibility), consistent with NASBLA-aligned course curricula

question: Why is water temperature relevant to choosing a PFD on Missouri's larger lakes, such as the Lake of the Ozarks, especially in early spring?
choice_a: Cold water dramatically speeds the onset of hypothermia and can cause cold-water shock that impairs swimming ability within minutes, so wearing a PFD at all times is especially important when water is cold even if air temperature feels warm
choice_b: Cold water has no effect on swimming ability or PFD need
choice_c: PFDs are not needed once water temperature exceeds 50 degrees Fahrenheit
choice_d: Only inflatable PFDs work in cold water
explanation: Water temperature can lag well behind air temperature in spring, and Missouri reservoirs can be dangerously cold even on a warm day; cold-water immersion can cause involuntary gasping and rapid loss of swimming ability, making a worn PFD critical even when conditions on land feel mild.
source_note: Universal boating safety fundamentals (cold-water immersion), applied to Missouri reservoir conditions

question: Why do most boating safety courses recommend wearing a PFD at all times rather than just keeping it stowed on board?
choice_a: Wearing a PFD is only required while docked
choice_b: Most drowning victims in boating accidents are found not wearing a PFD, and a capsizing or fall overboard often happens too suddenly to put one on afterward
choice_c: PFDs are more effective when left in a storage locker
choice_d: There is no safety benefit to wearing a PFD before an emergency happens
explanation: National boating-accident statistics consistently show most drowning victims were not wearing a PFD; because falls overboard and capsizings often happen suddenly and without warning, there is frequently no time to locate and put one on after the emergency starts.
source_note: Universal boating safety fundamentals (PFD wear rate and drowning statistics), consistent with NASBLA-aligned course curricula
